seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: My father asks you to excuse him for delay in replying but we are leaving this flat in a few weeks and he has been rather busy packing away books, pictures and manuscripts. He says that you may print any verses you like on Chamber Music provided that Mr. Jonathan Cape also agrees and that due acknowledgement is made. He has not seen the Tatler but will order a copy to-morrow.

div.note: JJ evidently directed his daughter Lucia (1907-1982) to write this letter for him.

In April 1931, JJ and family moved out of 2 square Robiac, 192 rue de Grenelle, where they had lived for nearly five years, and stayed in a series of hotels and flats in Paris, London, and other cities before settling into a small, furnished flat at 2 avenue St. Philibert, in Passy, in October 1931.

note.p: Pound had written JJ (“Dear Jayzuss”) from Rapallo on 24 January 1931 to ask if a Milan publisher, Giovanni Scheiwiller, could reprint JJ’s poem “I Hear an Army,” from Chamber Music (1907), in an anthology of twentieth-century English and American poetry, for the purpose of “orienting a few of the better Italian writers [who] are beginning to substitute english for french, or at least to include it in their concept of contemporaneity” (Robert Spoo, “Unpublished Letters of Ezra Pound to James, Nora, and Stanislaus Joyce,” James Joyce Quarterly, vol. 32, no. 3-4 [Spring-Summer 1995]: 555-56). The poem duly appeared in the privately printed volume, Profile: An Anthology Collected in MCMXXXI (Milan, 1932), limited to 250 numbered copies. Pound, Padraic Colum, W.B. Yeats, William Carlos Williams, Marianne Moore, Mina Loy, T.S. Eliot, and other poets also appeared in the volume. Pound considered it a “collection of poems which have stuck in my memory and which may possibly define their epoch, or at least rectify current ideas of it in respect to at least one contour” (note by Pound, Profile, recto of first leaf). Pound considered “I Hear an Army” to be an important Irish example of the clear, unrhetorical qualities of Imagism, and had earlier included it in Des Imagistes: An Anthology (New York: Albert and Charles Boni, 1914).

Giovanni Scheiwiller (1889-1965) worked for the Milan publishing firm of Ulrico Hoepli (1847-1935) but also published limited editions on his own. Pound described him affectionately as “employee, publisher and messenger boy” (The Selected Letters of Ezra Pound, 1907-1941, ed. D.D. Paige [New York: New Directions, 1971], 220), and told Louis Zukofsky that he was a “good guy/ ought to be NNNNcouraged” (Pound/Zukofsky: Selected Letters of Ezra Pound and Louis Zukofsky, ed. Barry Ahearn [New York: New Directions, 1987], 126). Scheiwiller admired Pound’s work and published his Confucius: Digest of the Analects in 1937. Scheiwiller’s son, Vanni, carried on the firm and issued many works by Pound in later years.

div.note: The first two English editions of JJ’s Chamber Music were published by Elkin Mathews of London (1907, 1918), the third by the Egoist Press of London (1923). In 1924, the volume was acquired by Jonathan Cape, Ltd., of London, which issued its first edition of the work in 1927, with further printings in 1934, 1943, 1945, and later (John J. Slocum and Herbert Cahoon, A Bibliography of James Joyce [New Haven: Yale University Press, 1953], 9-10). Herbert Jonathan Cape (1879-1960) founded the firm with Wren Howard in 1921, going on to publish works by H.G. Wells, W.H. Davies, Samuel Butler, Sinclair Lewis, Ernest Hemingway, Margaret Mead, and other authors. Cape also acquired Dubliners, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, and Exiles from the Egoist Press in 1924.

The Tatler was an English weekly magazine founded in 1901 by the British journalist Clement Shorter (1857-1926). By 1931, it was a shilling photo-journal, heavy on advertisements for brandies and cigarettes, expensive automobiles, stylish clothing and corsetry, and offering content that pandered to consumers of fashion, high society, gossip, tony weddings and social gatherings, movie stars, foxhunting (“the recent shoot”), and the horsey set. Pound refers to a “slick guy” reading (or not reading) “The Tatler” in Canto 19, first published in 1925-1926, a section of Pound’s epic poem that records snatches of dialogue and anecdotes illustrating economic abuse and exploitation in early twentieth-century Britain and America (The Cantos [New York: New Directions, 1995], 85).
